newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines settle land claims over big zinc mine.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines settle land claims over big zinc mine.

text.p: Aborigines, miners and politicians gave a green light on Wednesday to Australia's Century zinc mine, which promises to be one of the world's biggest.
The long-awaited agreement to go ahead with the A$1 billion (US$776 million) mine fell into place when the Queensland state government finally added its signature to the pact.

Under the agreement, Aborigines settled their claims for indigenous land title to the mine site in northern Australia in return for a total of A$90 million in aid from the mine's new owner, Pasminco Ltd, and the Queensland government.
Pasminco, a major world zinc producer, agreed to buy Century from global miner RTZ-CRA in January for A$345 million, pending the settlement of claims for indigenous land title.
"This is obviously a happy day and a long sought-after day for a great many people who have worked to this end," Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge said after approving the agreement.
The Century project, stalled for over a year by talks with Aborigines, had become a symbol to conservative politicians and mining companies of problems with indigenous land title.
A new and evolving concept, Australia's system of indigenous or native title has been criticised as a frustrating process which is bogging down investment in the mining industry.
The agreement comes as Aborigines confront the huge pastoral industry over the same issue, after the High Court extended the concept of native title to cover pastoral leases as well.
Pasminco, which will take over the Century project once the mining lease and other approvals are given, plans to bring the mine into production in 1999.
The mine is forecast to produce annually 780,000 tonnes of zinc concentrate, destined for Pasminco's Budel smelter in the Netherlands.
